strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: adapting web agents to target environments with synthetic supervision, avoiding expensive human annotation and test-task leakage.

Proposes a clear and well-motivated framework, SynthAgent, with dual refinement of tasks and trajectories: categorized exploration, task refinement during collection, offline trajectory refinement, and supervised fine-tuning.

Experiments are extensive on WebArena across five websites, with multiple synthetic baselines (Self-Instruct, OS-Genesis, Explorer), an SFT reference, two open-source base models, ablations, scaling analysis, case studies, and full prompt templates in the appendix.

Main results show substantial gains over synthetic baselines: Qwen +Ours 20.80 vs OS-Genesis 13.27 and Self-Instruct 11.50; UI-TARS +Ours 17.26 vs OS-Genesis 14.60, supporting the value of the proposed refinement pipeline.
Ablation and data-quality analyses provide useful evidence that trajectory refinement is the key component and that dual refinement reduces noise/hallucinations relative to baselines.
weaknesses: The paper overclaims adaptation to 'new websites'/'new environments': synthesis and evaluation use the same five WebArena websites, so no truly unseen website or cross-website generalization is demonstrated. The agent has access to the target environment during synthesis, which limits the novelty of the 'new environment' claim.

Critical evaluation metrics rely on LLM-as-a-judge (GPT-4.1) for task quality, diversity, trajectory quality, and completion rates, without human validation or evidence that these judge scores correlate with final agent success. This is potentially circular because GPT-4.1 is also used to generate and refine the synthetic data.

No statistical significance, variance, or error bars are reported; all main results appear to be single runs. WebArena agent performance can be high-variance, so the robustness of the reported improvements is unclear.

The 'SFT upper bound' is mislabeled and internally inconsistent: for Qwen, SFT on test tasks (16.37) is lower than SynthAgent (20.80), while for UI-TARS, SynthAgent (17.26) is below SFT (23.45). The description of using the full 812 tasks for SFT also raises possible leakage/interpretation issues that are not resolved.

Reproducibility is incomplete: code is only promised, random seeds and optimizer details are absent, and trajectory refinement edits are not re-executed or verified for executability after reordering/deletion, leaving a risk that refined trajectories contain artifacts.

The paper lacks a limitations section and broader impact discussion, and does not analyze failure modes of the final adapted agent or the practical gap to stronger proprietary models such as GPT-4.1 (25.22 overall).

strengths: Addresses a relevant and challenging problem: adapting web agents to unseen environments with synthetic supervision, avoiding human annotation and test-task leakage.

Proposes a sensible four-stage framework (categorized exploration, task refinement during trajectory collection, trajectory refinement, SFT) with dual refinement targeting hallucinated tasks and noisy trajectories.
Provides a reasonably thorough empirical study on WebArena across two open-source models and multiple synthetic-data baselines, with consistent gains over Self-Instruct, OS-Genesis, and Explorer.
Includes useful ablation and analysis: component contributions, data scaling, synthetic data quality/diversity, trajectory completion rates, and cost comparisons.
Offers detailed prompts and implementation details in the appendix, and the use of WebArena Docker environments supports reproducibility in principle.
The core claims are generally supported by the experiments: synthetic data quality improves, and fine-tuning on refined data outperforms existing synthetic-data methods.
weaknesses: The 'SFT upper bound' is inconsistent: on Qwen, SynthAgent reaches 20.80 while SFT trained on test-set tasks only reaches 16.37, undermining the claimed upper-bound interpretation and raising questions about training data quantity, task overlap, or evaluation protocol.

Baseline reimplementation, especially Explorer, is questionable; its very low performance (4.44/4.96) and 68.3% budget-exceedance rate may reflect implementation choices rather than the original method's capabilities.

The quality and diversity analyses rely heavily on GPT-4.1 as an LLM judge, with no human validation or inter-annotator agreement; since GPT-4.1 is also used for synthesis and refinement, this introduces potential circularity.
No statistical significance tests or variance across runs are reported; the main results are single evaluations on 226 tasks, so the robustness of the reported gains is unclear.
The evaluation is limited to WebArena and two 7B-scale models; broader claims about web agent adaptation and generalization to other environments are not fully established.
The code is not yet available, and reliance on proprietary GPT-4.1 for synthesis/refinement limits reproducibility over time and may make cost/scalability claims difficult to verify.
The methodological novelty is incremental over OS-Genesis and Explorer; categorized exploration and LLM-based refinement are reasonable but not deeply new.
No limitations section or thorough discussion of failure modes, LLM dependency, and computational cost is provided.

strengths: Addresses a relevant and timely problem: adapting web agents to new environments with synthetic supervision, avoiding human-annotated task data and test-task leakage.
Proposes a clear and well-motivated four-stage pipeline combining categorized exploration, task refinement during collection, post-hoc trajectory refinement, and supervised fine-tuning.
Evaluates on WebArena with two open-source multimodal agents (Qwen2.5-VL-7B and UI-TARS-1.5-7B) and compares against multiple synthetic-data baselines and an oracle SFT upper bound.
Includes an ablation study isolating categorized exploration, task refinement, and trajectory refinement, showing that trajectory refinement is particularly important for downstream performance.
Provides extensive implementation details, action space, prompt templates, case studies, and API-cost analysis, which improves transparency and potential reproducibility.
Goes beyond a single success-rate table with data-scaling analysis, t-SNE task diversity visualization, and trajectory completion statistics.
Reports overall gains over prior synthetic-data methods for Qwen2.5-VL and overall gains for UI-TARS, indicating practical promise of the synthetic supervision approach.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the method heavily builds on OS-Genesis and Explorer, and dual refinement is largely a combination of existing task-refinement and post-hoc trajectory-editing ideas rather than a substantial conceptual advance.

The central claim of adapting to new environments is not fully tested: synthesis and evaluation are performed on the same five WebArena websites, and no truly held-out website/environment experiment is provided.

Results are single-run success rates with no variance, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, despite LLM-based agents being stochastic and the reported gains being modest in places.

Data quality and diversity claims rely solely on GPT-4.1 as an LLM judge, the same model used for synthesis/refinement, with no human evaluation or validation that LLM judgments correlate with human judgments.

Trajectory refinement uses an LLM to edit trajectories without execution verification; it may remove necessary steps or reorder incorrectly, and the paper does not independently verify that refined trajectories are executable or correct.

The paper overstates consistency: for UI-TARS, OS-Genesis outperforms SynthAgent on some websites (e.g., Shopping) and ties on others, contradicting claims of consistently outperforming all baselines.

Baselines may be under-tuned or unfairly configured; Explorer’s very low performance is attributed to its design, but it is reimplemented with GPT-4.1 and may require more careful tuning or different prompting.
Data-scaling analysis shows Map performance peaking at 40% data and then degrading, but this potential overfitting/noise issue is not explained or addressed.

Reproducibility is limited: code is not available in the submission ('will be publicly available'), and the method depends on closed-source GPT-4.1, whose API may change and which also serves as the judge.
The paper does not compare against several recent synthetic-data methods for web agents discussed in related work (e.g., AgentTrek, WebSynth, Learn-by-Interact), narrowing the empirical picture.

Some claims are overbroad: 'fully synthetic supervision' still relies on a proprietary LLM and human-designed prompts/heuristics, and 'without human involvement' refers only to task/trajectory collection, not to the overall pipeline design.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: adapting web agents to new environments without costly human-annotated task demonstrations.

Proposes a coherent synthetic supervision pipeline with dual refinement (task refinement during execution and trajectory refinement post hoc) that directly targets task hallucinations and trajectory noise.
Reports extensive experiments across WebArena and Online-Mind2Web, including ablations, data-scaling analysis, trajectory-quality comparisons, cost analysis, and qualitative case studies.
Provides detailed implementation information, action space, prompts, and category sets in the appendix, which supports reproducibility and reimplementation.
Demonstrates consistent gains over synthetic-data baselines and competitive performance on a live benchmark, while using lower API cost than the Explorer baseline.
Evaluates with multiple base models and multiple LLM judges, strengthening the empirical case relative to a single-model/single-judge setup.
weaknesses: The claimed SFT upper bound is inconsistent: on WebArena with Qwen, SynthAgent (20.80) outperforms SFT (16.37), so SFT cannot be an upper bound; the text also says SynthAgent shows a closer gap to SFT, which is not true for Qwen.

There are table/text inconsistencies: the diversity numbers cited in the main text (e.g., OS-Genesis 83, Explorer 54) do not match Table 3, and Table 3 shows the ablated w/o TR model has higher diversity than the full model, contradicting the claim that SynthAgent achieves the highest diversity.
Quality and diversity assessments rely heavily on LLM-as-a-judge, with no human validation; this is a significant concern because the same or related LLMs are used for synthesis and evaluation.

Baseline reimplementation, especially Explorer, may not be entirely faithful; its very poor performance could stem from implementation or hyperparameter choices rather than the method's inherent limitations.
The code URL is missing in the manuscript, and the method depends on proprietary GPT-4.1/GPT-5.1 models, limiting full reproducibility and external validation.

The contribution is largely incremental: categorized exploration, conflict-triggered task refinement, and post-hoc trajectory refinement are each related to prior work, and the novelty lies mainly in combining and tuning them.
No statistical significance tests or variance estimates are reported for the main results, making it difficult to assess the reliability of small differences across methods.

Some claims are overstated or insufficiently supported, e.g., 'fully synthetic supervision' still relies on carefully human-designed prompts and proprietary LLMs, and the generalization claim is based on LLM-judge outcomes without human verification.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: adapting web agents to new environments with fully synthetic supervision, avoiding costly human annotation and test-task leakage.

Clearly identifies a real design tension in prior work—environment grounding during execution improves task quality but introduces trajectory noise—and proposes a well-motivated dual refinement strategy (task refinement during collection plus post-hoc trajectory refinement).

Provides strong empirical evidence across two benchmarks (WebArena and Online-Mind2Web) and two open-source models (Qwen2.5-VL-7B and UI-TARS-1.5-7B), with multiple baselines and consistent gains over existing synthetic-data methods.

Thorough analysis and ablations validate each component (categorized exploration, task refinement, trajectory refinement), and additional studies on data quality, diversity, trajectory completion rates, cost, and scaling strengthen the claims.
Good reproducibility: code is public, prompts and implementation details are included in the appendix, and the evaluation setup is described clearly.
weaknesses: The framework relies on a proprietary LLM (GPT-4.1) for task synthesis, refinement, and LLM-as-judge evaluation. Although multiple judges are used, the lack of human evaluation and dependence on closed models may limit reproducibility and introduce model-specific biases.

The SFT-on-test-set baseline is described as an 'informative upper bound', but on Qwen, SynthAgent (20.80) outperforms it (16.37). This inconsistency is not explained and raises questions about the baseline's validity or the upper-bound claim.

The paper claims to outperform 'existing synthetic data methods' but only compares against Self-Instruct, OS-Genesis, and Explorer. Relevant recent web-agent data synthesis methods (e.g., AgentTrek, Synatra, WebSynthesis, NNetNav) are discussed but not empirically compared.
WebArena evaluation uses a subset of 226 tasks and excludes cross-website navigation, which may limit comparability with prior work that uses the full 812-task benchmark.

Some design choices (e.g., sampling up to 2 unvisited elements per category, context window of 3) are set empirically without ablation, and the scaling analysis shows non-monotonic behavior for the Maps environment that is not fully explained.

The Explorer baseline performs very poorly, even degrading the base model. While the authors provide evidence of a faithful reimplementation, such a weak baseline can inflate relative gains and warrants caution.

strengths: The paper targets a well-motivated and practically important problem: adapting web agents to unseen environments without test-task leakage or human annotation, and the dual-refinement framing (task refinement to preserve feasibility, trajectory refinement to remove induced noise) is coherent and clearly articulated.
The method is described concretely across four stages, and all prompts (Tables 7-12) are provided in the appendix, which materially aids reproducibility and is better than much of the related work.

The empirical package is reasonably broad: two benchmarks (offline WebArena and online Online-Mind2Web), two base agents (Qwen2.5-VL-7B, UI-TARS-1.5-7B), three LLM judges, an ablation, a data-scaling study, and qualitative case studies.

Gains over the strongest synthetic baseline (OS-Genesis) are directionally consistent across both models and across most individual websites, and the diagnostic in Table 4 (trajectory completion/exceeded-budget rates and API cost) usefully explains why continuous task refinement fails.
The scaling curve (Figure 4) and the cost analysis provide some evidence that the pipeline is not merely exploiting a single environment.
weaknesses: No variance, error bars, or significance testing is reported anywhere; all results appear to be single runs. Given ~55 tasks per website, ablation differences such as 3.54% vs 3.99% vs 4.87% are plausibly within noise, so the repeated claim that SynthAgent "substantially outperforms" baselines is not supported at that granularity.

Internal inconsistency: Section 5.1 states SynthAgent achieves "the highest diversity score after task refinement," but Table 3 reports SynthAgent 82 vs. OS-Genesis 83 (and the same text first concedes OS-Genesis achieves better diversity). The claim is contradicted by the authors' own table.

Several numbers look suspiciously coincident across tables: the w/o TR and w/o TR&JR ablation rows for Qwen share the same overall (15.93) despite very different per-site values (Shopping 16.37 vs 20.00, Maps 18.75 vs 12.50), and the w/o CE overall (17.26) equals the UI-TARS +Ours overall (17.26). This raises concerns about transcription/result-integrity that reviewers cannot resolve.

An anomalous headline result is left unexplained: for Qwen, synthetic-data "Ours" (20.80) exceeds "+SFT" trained on the actual test-set tasks (16.37), while for UI-TARS the pattern completely inverts (17.26 vs. 23.45). A synthetic method beating test-task supervision on one model and falling six points short on another demands analysis, but none is offered; this asymmetry also undermines the claim of a "consistent" advantage.

Evaluation circularity: GPT-4.1 is simultaneously the synthesis model, the model used to re-implement all baselines, and the primary judge for task quality, trajectory quality, and the Online-Mind2Web benchmark. The additional GPT-5.1/Qwen3-30B judges help, but "diversity" scores (Table 3) remain model-generated opinions rather than grounded metrics.

Baseline fidelity is questionable. Explorer is re-implemented (and even augmented with authentication support absent from the original) yet scores 4.44/4.96, well below the untuned base model (8.80/8.85). A baseline that degrades the base model is a classic symptom of implementation artifacts; the authors' assertion that this "matches the algorithmic design" is not independently verifiable.

The evaluation protocol departs from standard WebArena (only 226 of 812 tasks, cross-website tasks excluded), which prevents comparison against published numbers, and the online benchmark is judged entirely by LLM-as-judge with no human evaluation.

Novelty is modest and incremental: categorized exploration (group elements, sample up to two per category), conflict-triggered refinement, and post-hoc LLM trajectory editing are close variants of components already present in OS-Genesis, Explorer, and NNetNav-style trajectory labeling. The "critical tension" framing is plausible but asserted rather than rigorously demonstrated.

Key hyperparameters (at most 2 elements sampled per category, context window of 3, step budget of 30) are set without sensitivity analysis, and the abstract's code link ("publicly available at") is empty; combined with reliance on proprietary GPT-4.1 and live websites, exact reproducibility of the reported numbers is doubtful.
